chapters.title: Chapter 1: What Are Derivatives and Why Do They Exist?

lessons.title: What Really Happens When You Trade a Futures Contract

children.text: Most retail traders who trade Nifty futures have no idea what they are actually doing when they click buy. They think they are buying Nifty. They are not. They are entering into a legally binding obligation to buy a specific quantity of Nifty at a specific price on a specific future date. And on the other side of that trade, someone has a legally binding obligation to sell. Understanding this distinction between buying a stock and entering a futures contract is the foundation of everything that follows in this course.
The Two Sides of Every Futures Trade

When you buy a Nifty futures contract, you are the long side. You have agreed to buy the Nifty index at today's futures price on the expiry date. The person on the other side is short. They have agreed to sell Nifty at that same price on expiry. Neither of you is exchanging money for Nifty right now. You are both posting margin as a security deposit and agreeing to settle the difference in cash at expiry based on where Nifty actually trades.

body.text: In Indian equity futures, almost no contracts result in actual delivery of shares. Over 99 percent are cash settled. The difference between the futures price you locked in and the final settlement price is credited or debited to your account. You never actually buy or sell the underlying asset.

children.text: Why Derivatives Were Invented

Derivatives were not invented for speculation. They were invented to transfer risk. A wheat farmer who will harvest in 3 months does not know what price wheat will fetch. A flour mill that needs wheat in 3 months does not know what it will cost. A futures contract allows them to agree on a price today, eliminating uncertainty for both parties. The farmer locks in revenue. The mill locks in costs. Both reduce risk. This is hedging — the original and still primary purpose of derivatives.

In Indian capital markets, the same logic applies. An institution holding a large equity portfolio uses Nifty futures to hedge against a market decline. An importer expecting a dollar payment in 3 months uses currency futures to lock in the exchange rate. The speculator provides the liquidity that makes these hedges possible. Without speculators willing to take the other side, hedgers would have no counterparty.

body.title: Apply It: Understand Your Next Futures Trade
steps: Go to NSE website and look up the current Nifty 50 futures contract
Note the lot size, the current futures price, and the expiry date
Calculate the full contract value: lot size multiplied by current futures price
Find the current margin required for one lot on Zerodha Margin Calculator
Divide margin by contract value to get your leverage ratio
Write down: if Nifty moves 1%, what is your profit or loss in rupees on one lot?

lessons.title: Futures vs Options vs Forwards vs Swaps — The Derivatives Family

children.text: The word derivative covers a wide family of financial instruments, and the differences between them matter enormously for how they are used and who uses them. Retail traders in India primarily encounter futures and options on NSE. But the derivatives universe is far larger — forwards, swaps, and exotic structures underpin trillions of dollars in global transactions daily.
Futures vs Forwards

A futures contract is standardised and exchange-traded. The lot size, expiry date, and settlement mechanism are fixed by NSE. A forward contract is customised and traded directly between two parties over the counter, with no exchange involvement. An Indian exporter and a bank might agree on a forward contract for a specific dollar amount at a specific rate on a specific date — none of those parameters are fixed by anyone else.

body.text: The key difference: futures have daily mark-to-market settlement and are cleared through a central clearinghouse, eliminating counterparty risk. Forwards have no daily settlement and carry counterparty risk. If the other party defaults, you have a problem. This is why futures are safer for retail participants.

children.text: Options vs Futures

The critical distinction between options and futures is obligation versus right. A futures buyer is obligated to honour the contract at expiry. An options buyer has the right but not the obligation — they can let the option expire worthless. This asymmetry means options buyers have limited downside with potentially unlimited upside. Futures traders have unlimited downside in both directions.
Swaps

Swaps are agreements to exchange cash flows. The most common is an interest rate swap — one party pays fixed interest, the other pays floating interest, and they swap the difference periodically. Indian corporations use interest rate swaps to manage borrowing costs. Currency swaps allow companies to exchange debt obligations in different currencies. Retail traders rarely access swaps directly, but they underpin a significant portion of the global financial system.

body.title: Apply It: Map the Derivatives Universe
steps: Go to NSE website and list all derivative products available — equity futures, index futures, currency futures
For each category, identify who would use it as a hedger versus who uses it as a speculator
Look up the total open interest in Nifty futures and Bank Nifty futures on any given day
Compare the open interest in equity futures vs equity options — which is larger?
Research one example of an Indian company using an interest rate swap in their annual report notes

lessons.title: Who Uses Futures? — Hedgers, Speculators and Arbitrageurs

children.text: Every futures market has three types of participants, and each plays a different and necessary role. Remove any one of the three and the market stops functioning properly. Understanding which category you fall into — and which category the person on the other side of your trade likely falls into — is fundamental to trading intelligently.
Hedgers

Hedgers use futures to reduce existing risk. A mutual fund with a large equity portfolio sells Nifty futures to protect against a market decline. An IT company expecting dollar revenues in 6 months buys dollar futures to lock in the current exchange rate. A gold jeweller who has committed to a fixed price buys gold futures to protect against a rise in gold prices before delivery.

body.text: Hedgers are willing to accept a slightly worse expected outcome in exchange for reduced uncertainty. The mutual fund that sells Nifty futures does not expect to profit from the hedge — they are paying for insurance. If markets rise, the hedge costs them money. That cost is acceptable because it buys certainty.

children.text: Speculators and Arbitrageurs

Speculators take on risk willingly in exchange for the opportunity to profit from price movements. Most retail F&O traders are speculators. They have no underlying position to hedge — they are simply betting on the direction of the market. Speculators provide the liquidity that makes it possible for hedgers to find counterparties quickly and at fair prices.

Arbitrageurs exploit price discrepancies between related instruments. In Indian markets, the most common form is cash-futures arbitrage: when Nifty futures trade at a significant premium to spot Nifty, arbitrageurs buy the spot basket and sell futures simultaneously, locking in a risk-free profit. This activity forces the futures price back toward fair value and keeps markets efficient.

body.title: Apply It: Identify Participant Types
steps: On any trading day, check NSE FII derivatives data — what is the net position of FIIs in index futures?
Are FIIs net long or net short? Are they speculating or hedging their equity portfolio?
Check DIIs futures position — typically opposite to FIIs
Look up current Nifty spot price and Nifty futures price — is there a premium or discount?
Calculate the annualised cost of carry implied by this premium
Identify whether the current premium makes cash-futures arbitrage attractive

lessons.title: Lot Size, Tick Size and Contract Value — The Numbers You Must Know

children.text: Before placing a single futures trade, you must understand three numbers: lot size, tick size, and contract value. These determine exactly how much money you make or lose with every price movement. Retail traders who skip this understanding routinely take positions far larger than they intend, leading to catastrophic losses when markets move against them.
Lot Size and Tick Size

NSE sets the lot size for each futures contract. You cannot trade half a lot. The minimum is one lot. Nifty 50 futures currently have a lot size of 25. Bank Nifty has a lot size of 15. Individual stock futures have lot sizes that vary by company. NSE periodically revises lot sizes to keep contract values within a reasonable range. Tick size is the minimum price movement — for Nifty futures, this is 0.05 points. Each tick movement in your favour earns you lot size multiplied by tick size.

body.text: NSE targets a minimum contract value of approximately 5 to 10 lakh rupees per lot. When a stock's price rises significantly, NSE reduces the lot size so the contract remains accessible. Always check the current lot size before trading — it changes, and calculating P&L on outdated lot size information leads to errors.

children.text: Contract Value

Contract value is lot size multiplied by current futures price. If Nifty futures are at 22000 and lot size is 25, contract value is 5.5 lakh rupees. This is the notional exposure you are taking on with one lot. Always know your contract value before entering — it tells you the true scale of your position relative to your capital.

body.title: Apply It: Calculate Contract Values
steps: Go to NSE website and find the current lot sizes for Nifty 50, Bank Nifty, and any 3 individual stock futures
For each, find the current futures price and calculate the full contract value
Calculate: if Nifty moves 100 points, what is the P&L on one lot?
Calculate: if Bank Nifty moves 200 points, what is the P&L on one lot?
Using current margin requirements, calculate the leverage ratio for each contract
Assess: with your current capital, how many lots can you trade while keeping a 30% buffer above minimum margin?

lessons.title: Margin — SPAN, Exposure, and How Much Money You Actually Need

children.text: Margin is the deposit you post with your broker to hold a futures position. It is not a down payment — you are not buying anything. It is collateral that ensures you can honour your daily settlement obligations. Understanding margin is critical because it determines your actual leverage and your risk of receiving a margin call.
SPAN Margin

SPAN stands for Standard Portfolio Analysis of Risk. It is the minimum margin required by the exchange, calculated by NSE's clearing corporation using a complex risk model. SPAN margin estimates the maximum possible loss on your position over a single trading day under stressed market conditions. It changes daily as volatility changes — during high-volatility periods like budget day or major global events, SPAN margin can increase significantly.
Exposure Margin

In addition to SPAN margin, brokers collect exposure margin — an additional buffer above the SPAN requirement. This protects the broker against losses beyond what SPAN covers in extreme scenarios. Total margin required is SPAN plus exposure margin combined. Zerodha and most Indian brokers show both components separately in their margin calculators.

body.text: SEBI's peak margin rules require that your margin be sufficient throughout the trading day, not just at the start. If your position moves against you intraday, your broker may square off your position without warning if your margin falls below the required level. Always maintain a buffer of 20 to 30 percent above the minimum margin requirement.

body.title: Apply It: Calculate Margin Requirements
steps: Go to Zerodha Margin Calculator at zerodha.com/margin-calculator
Calculate the margin required for 1 lot of Nifty futures
Calculate for 1 lot of Bank Nifty futures
Calculate for 1 lot of any stock futures you are interested in
For each, calculate leverage: contract value divided by margin required
Determine: with your current capital, how many lots can you trade while keeping 30% buffer above minimum margin?

lessons.title: Mark-to-Market — Why Futures Are Settled Daily

children.text: One of the most important features of futures — and one that consistently surprises new traders — is daily mark-to-market settlement. Unlike stocks where you can hold a losing position indefinitely waiting for recovery, futures contracts are settled every single day. Your profit or loss is not theoretical — it is credited or debited to your account at the end of each trading session.
How MTM Works

At the end of each trading day, NSE calculates the settlement price — typically the weighted average price of the futures contract in the last 30 minutes of trading. Every open position is marked to this settlement price. If you are long Nifty at 22000 and the settlement price is 22150, you receive 150 points multiplied by lot size 25 = 3,750 rupees credited to your account. Your new effective entry price for the next day becomes 22150, not 22000.

body.text: MTM settlement is why futures trading requires active capital management. If Nifty falls 300 points against your long position over 3 days, you have already lost 7,500 rupees in real cash — not a paper loss. Your margin account has been debited. If the debit brings your balance below the minimum margin, you face a margin call before the fourth day's opening.

children.text: MTM vs Options Premium

Options buyers pay premium upfront and can hold until expiry without any additional cash requirement — the maximum loss is the premium already paid. Futures traders face daily MTM debits that can exceed their initial margin if the market moves sharply. A futures position that moves 5 percent against you in 3 days can wipe your entire margin and trigger additional calls.

body.title: Apply It: Simulate MTM Settlement
steps: Take any 5 consecutive trading days of Nifty closing prices from the past month
Assume you bought 1 lot of Nifty futures at the first day's closing price
Calculate daily MTM: each day's closing price minus the previous day's closing price, multiplied by 25
Sum the daily MTM credits and debits over 5 days
Is your total P&L the same as simply taking the difference between day 1 and day 5 price multiplied by lot size?
What is the minimum account balance you would need to survive the worst daily MTM debit without a margin call?

lessons.title: Expiry and Rollover — How Traders Carry Positions Forward

children.text: Every futures contract has a fixed expiry date. In India, equity and index futures expire on the last Thursday of each month. There are always three contracts available simultaneously — near month (current month), mid month (next month), and far month (the month after). When the near month expires, the mid month becomes the new near month, and a new far month contract is created.
What Happens at Expiry

If you hold a futures position to expiry without rolling, it is cash-settled at the final settlement price — the average spot price of the underlying in the last 30 minutes of trading on expiry day. You receive or pay the difference between your entry price and the final settlement price. Most active traders avoid holding to expiry because the final settlement price can differ from the last traded futures price, creating basis risk.
Rolling a Position

Rolling means closing the expiring near-month contract and simultaneously opening the same position in the next-month contract. If you are long 1 lot of Nifty near-month futures, you sell 1 lot of near-month and buy 1 lot of mid-month. The cost of rolling is the price difference between the two contracts. If mid-month futures trade at a premium to near-month, you pay that premium each time you roll.

body.text: Rollover data — the percentage of near-month open interest that has moved to the next month — is a widely watched market signal. High rollover with a significant long bias implies bullishness for the next month. Low rollover suggests traders are not confident about direction and are choosing not to carry positions forward.

body.title: Apply It: Analyse Rollover Data
steps: Go to NSE website and check the open interest in near-month and mid-month Nifty futures
Calculate: what percentage of total open interest is in the near month vs mid month?
Check rollover statistics on Moneycontrol or Sensibull
Is the current rollover percentage above or below the 3-month average?
What does the rollover cost tell you about market direction sentiment?
Calculate the annualised rollover cost if you had to roll a position every month for a year

lessons.title: Fair Value of a Futures Contract — Cost of Carry Model

children.text: Futures prices are not random. They are mathematically derived from the current spot price of the underlying asset, adjusted for the cost of carrying that position until expiry. This is called the cost of carry model, and it tells you exactly what a futures contract should theoretically trade at. When the actual futures price deviates significantly from this theoretical fair value, arbitrage opportunities emerge and are quickly exploited.
The Formula

Fair Value of Futures equals Spot Price multiplied by (1 + Risk-Free Rate multiplied by Time to Expiry) minus Expected Dividends during the period. The risk-free rate is typically the 91-day T-bill rate or repo rate. Time to expiry is expressed as a fraction of a year. If Nifty spot is at 22000, the risk-free rate is 6.5 percent, and there are 30 days to expiry, fair value is approximately 22000 multiplied by (1 + 0.065 multiplied by 30 divided by 365) = 22,117.

body.text: The difference between the futures price and fair value tells you about market sentiment. If futures trade above fair value, it implies positive cost of carry — bulls are willing to pay extra to hold the position forward. If futures trade below fair value in backwardation, bears are dominant and sellers are willing to discount the contract to find buyers.

children.text: In practice, the futures premium decreases as expiry approaches. With 30 days to expiry, futures might trade at a 100-point premium to spot. With 5 days to expiry, the premium collapses to 15 to 20 points. On expiry day, futures and spot converge — they must trade at the same price by definition.

body.title: Apply It: Calculate Fair Value
steps: Note the current Nifty spot price
Note the current repo rate from RBI website or 91-day T-bill yield
Find the number of days to current month Nifty futures expiry
Calculate fair value using the cost of carry formula
Compare with the actual Nifty futures price — is there a premium or discount?
Calculate the implied cost of carry — does it match current interest rates?

lessons.title: Basis — The Spread Between Spot and Futures

children.text: Basis is defined as the spot price minus the futures price. In normal conditions, futures trade at a premium to spot, making basis negative — futures price is higher than spot price. Basis narrows predictably as expiry approaches and reaches zero on expiry day. Traders who understand basis can extract information from its movements that others miss entirely.
What Basis Tells You

When basis narrows faster than expected — futures premium collapses before expiry — it typically signals unwinding of long positions. Traders who were long futures are exiting, reducing the premium. When basis expands — futures trade at an unusually large premium — it signals aggressive buying in futures relative to spot, implying institutional accumulation or speculative bullishness.

body.text: Watch for sudden basis changes in individual stock futures. If a stock's futures suddenly trade at a significant discount to spot, it often signals that large traders are aggressively shorting the stock — they are willing to sell at a discount to spot to express their bearish view. This can be an early warning of a price decline.

children.text: Basis Risk for Hedgers

A hedger using futures faces basis risk — the risk that the futures price does not move exactly with the spot price they are hedging. If you own 50 lakh worth of Nifty stocks and sell Nifty futures to hedge, the hedge is not perfect if your portfolio has a different composition from Nifty. The spot price of your portfolio might move differently from Nifty spot, creating residual unhedged risk.

body.title: Apply It: Track Basis Over Expiry Cycle
steps: For the next two weeks, record daily: Nifty spot price and Nifty near-month futures price
Calculate basis each day: spot price minus futures price
Plot the basis over the two weeks — does it narrow as expiry approaches?
On expiry day, note how close the final settlement price is to the last traded spot price
Calculate the average daily basis narrowing — this is the implied daily carry cost
Compare: is the implied carry cost consistent with current interest rates?

lessons.title: Contango vs Backwardation — What the Shape of the Futures Curve Tells You

children.text: When you look at the prices of near-month, mid-month, and far-month futures contracts simultaneously, you see a futures curve. The shape of this curve tells you something about market expectations, demand pressure, and sentiment that the spot price alone cannot reveal. Understanding contango and backwardation is essential for anyone trading futures beyond a single contract.
Contango — The Normal State

Contango occurs when futures prices are higher than the current spot price — far-month futures trade at a premium to near-month futures. This is the normal state for equity index futures because of positive cost of carry. Holding equity costs money (interest foregone), so far-month futures compensate by trading higher. In commodity markets, contango implies sufficient current supply.
Backwardation — The Stress Signal

Backwardation occurs when near-month futures trade at a premium to far-month futures — the futures curve slopes downward. For equity futures, backwardation is unusual and signals bearishness: market participants are willing to sell near-month futures at a higher price than far-month, implying they expect the market to fall. In commodity markets, backwardation signals immediate scarcity.

body.text: In Indian equity markets, when Nifty futures enter backwardation — near-month futures trading below spot — it is a strong bearish signal. It means institutional participants are actively shorting the near-month contract and bidding up the cost of near-term protection. Historically, periods of equity backwardation have often preceded significant market corrections.

body.title: Apply It: Read the Futures Curve
steps: On NSE website or Sensibull, check the prices of Nifty near-month, mid-month, and far-month futures
Is the curve in contango (upward sloping) or backwardation (downward sloping)?
Calculate the premium of each month over the previous month
Is the premium consistent with current interest rates, or larger or smaller than expected?
Check the same for Bank Nifty — does it show a different structure from Nifty?
Research: in what months in 2020 or 2022 did Indian equity futures show backwardation? What happened to markets?

lessons.title: Directional Trading with Nifty Futures — Long and Short

children.text: The simplest and most common use of Nifty futures is directional trading — taking a leveraged bet on whether the index will rise or fall. This is fundamentally different from buying a Nifty ETF or mutual fund. The leverage amplifies both profits and losses. The daily MTM settlement means a wrong-direction trade costs you real money every evening.
Going Long and Going Short

A long Nifty futures trade profits when Nifty rises. You buy 1 lot at 22000. Nifty rises to 22300. Your profit is 300 points multiplied by 25 = 7,500 rupees. Shorting Nifty futures is mechanically identical but in reverse. You sell 1 lot at 22000. If Nifty falls to 21700, you profit 300 points multiplied by 25 = 7,500 rupees. This is one of the significant advantages of futures over equity — you can profit from falling markets as easily as rising ones.

body.text: Never average a losing futures position. Adding to a long position as Nifty falls, or adding to a short as Nifty rises, dramatically increases your position size precisely when the market is telling you that you are wrong. This has blown up more retail futures accounts than any other single mistake.

children.text: Define your stop loss before entry — not after. Not when the trade moves against you. Before. And never widen a stop loss. The discipline to honour your stop is more important than any analysis of where Nifty is going.

body.title: Apply It: Paper Trade a Directional Setup
steps: Identify a technical setup on Nifty 50 daily chart — a support bounce, a breakout, or a moving average signal
Define your entry: the specific Nifty futures price at which you would buy or sell
Define your stop loss: the Nifty level at which the setup is invalidated
Define your target: the next significant resistance or support level
Calculate position size: how many lots can you trade with 2% risk of your paper-trading capital?
Track the trade for the next 5 sessions and record daily MTM settlement

lessons.title: Hedging Your Equity Portfolio Using Nifty Futures

children.text: If you hold a diversified Indian equity portfolio and are concerned about a near-term market correction, you do not need to sell all your stocks. You can sell Nifty futures to create a temporary hedge — a short position that gains as your portfolio falls. This is one of the most practical applications of futures for long-term equity investors and is routinely used by fund managers and sophisticated retail investors.
Calculating How Many Lots to Sell

The number of futures lots needed to hedge a portfolio depends on the portfolio's beta relative to Nifty. Beta measures how much your portfolio moves for every 1 percent move in Nifty. A portfolio with beta 1.2 moves 1.2 percent for every 1 percent Nifty move. The hedge formula: Number of lots = Portfolio Value multiplied by Portfolio Beta, divided by Nifty Futures Contract Value.

Example: Portfolio value 50 lakh, portfolio beta 1.1, Nifty futures at 22000, lot size 25. Contract value = 22000 multiplied by 25 = 5.5 lakh. Lots needed = (50 lakh multiplied by 1.1) divided by 5.5 lakh = 10 lots. Selling 10 lots of Nifty futures provides approximately full portfolio hedging.

body.text: A perfect hedge eliminates both downside and upside. If Nifty rises 5% after you hedge, your portfolio gains 5% but your short futures position loses 5% — you are flat. This is intentional. The hedge is insurance for when you are genuinely concerned about a correction. Remove the hedge when the concern passes.

body.title: Apply It: Design a Portfolio Hedge
steps: List 5 large-cap stocks you hold or would hypothetically hold, with their portfolio weights
Look up the beta of each stock relative to Nifty 50 on NSE website or Screener.in
Calculate the weighted average beta of your portfolio
Assume a portfolio value of 25 lakh rupees
Calculate the number of Nifty futures lots needed for a full hedge
Calculate the margin required for this hedge — is it capital-efficient?

lessons.title: Stock Futures — When to Use Them Instead of Equity

children.text: Individual stock futures allow you to take leveraged positions in specific companies without buying the underlying equity. This can be more capital-efficient than buying equity outright, but comes with its own considerations — dividend risk, rollover cost, liquidity, and the daily MTM settlement that equity holding does not require.
Advantages Over Equity

Stock futures require significantly less capital than buying equity. A 5-lakh equity position in Reliance requires 5 lakh rupees. The same notional exposure via Reliance futures might require only 1 to 1.5 lakh in margin. You can also easily short individual stocks through futures without the complexity of stock borrowing. For short-term traders with a specific view on a company, stock futures are a capital-efficient tool.

body.text: Dividend risk is unique to stock futures. When a company pays a dividend, the stock price falls by approximately the dividend amount on ex-dividend date. If you are long stock futures, this fall is fully reflected in your MTM loss. Unlike holding equity, you do not receive the dividend payment. Always check upcoming dividend dates before holding stock futures across the ex-dividend date.

children.text: Liquidity Considerations

Not all stock futures are equally liquid. Nifty and Bank Nifty futures are extremely liquid with tight bid-ask spreads. Large-cap stock futures have reasonable liquidity. Mid-cap stock futures can have wide spreads and thin volumes — entry and exit costs can be significant. Always check the bid-ask spread and average volume before trading any stock futures contract.

body.title: Apply It: Compare Stock Futures vs Equity
steps: Choose any Nifty 50 stock
Calculate the capital required to buy 500 shares of equity
Calculate the margin required for an equivalent notional exposure through futures
Compare the two — what is the capital saving from using futures?
Check the stock's upcoming dividend calendar on NSE website
Calculate the bid-ask spread as a percentage of price — is the futures contract liquid enough for your trade size?

lessons.title: Cash and Carry Arbitrage — A Risk-Free Trade?

children.text: Cash and carry arbitrage is often described as a risk-free trade, and in theory it is. In practice, it requires precise execution, sufficient capital, and an understanding of all the costs involved. When futures trade at a significant premium to fair value, arbitrageurs buy the spot basket and simultaneously sell futures, locking in the premium as profit with no directional risk.
The Mechanics

Example: Nifty spot is at 22000. Nifty futures expiring in 30 days are at 22200. Fair value is 22117 using 6.5% interest rate. The actual premium of 200 points exceeds fair value premium of 117 points by 83 points. An arbitrageur buys the Nifty spot basket and sells Nifty futures at 22200. At expiry, futures settle at spot. The arbitrageur gains approximately 83 points of risk-free profit minus transaction costs.

body.text: The costs that kill cash-carry arbitrage: brokerage on both legs, STT on equity delivery, impact cost of buying 50 stocks, opportunity cost of capital blocked for 30 days. In practice, the arbitrage is only profitable when the premium significantly exceeds fair value — typically by 50 to 100 basis points above normal. Algorithmic traders exploit these opportunities before manual traders can.

body.title: Apply It: Calculate Arbitrage Profitability
steps: Find current Nifty spot price and current Nifty near-month futures price
Calculate fair value using current repo rate and days to expiry
Calculate the excess premium: actual premium minus theoretical fair value premium
Estimate your total transaction costs: brokerage, STT, impact cost assume 0.1% of value
Calculate net arbitrage profit after costs
Annualise the return — is it better than parking the same capital in liquid funds?

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Risk, Rules and Famous Blowups

lessons.title: The Real Risk of Leverage — How Futures Traders Blow Up Accounts

children.text: Leverage is the most misunderstood concept in retail futures trading. It is presented as the feature — trade 5 lakh of Nifty with only 1 lakh of margin. What is not presented as clearly is the other side: a 2 percent adverse move in Nifty wipes 10 percent of your capital. A 10 percent adverse move over a week can destroy half your account. A 20 percent adverse move during a crisis like March 2020 could eliminate your entire capital and more.
The Mathematics of Ruin

Consider a trader with 5 lakh rupees trading 5 lots of Nifty futures. Contract value per lot at Nifty 22000 is 5.5 lakh, total exposure is 27.5 lakh — leverage of 5.5 times. Nifty falls 400 points (1.8%). Loss = 400 multiplied by 25 multiplied by 5 lots = 50,000 rupees, wiping 10% of capital in one day. This triggers a margin call. The trader adds more money. Nifty falls another 400 points. After two bad days, 20% of capital is gone.

body.text: SEBI data consistently shows that 90 percent of retail F&O traders lose money. The primary cause is not wrong direction calls — it is position sizing. Traders are using maximum possible leverage, which means one bad week is catastrophic. Professional traders use a fraction of their maximum possible leverage precisely to survive bad weeks.

children.text: The Rules That Keep Professionals Alive

Professional futures traders use four rules consistently. First, risk no more than 1 percent of capital per trade. Second, define the stop loss before entry and never move it further from entry. Third, never average into a losing futures position. Fourth, reduce position size after a losing streak — your judgement is impaired when you are down and trying to recover quickly.

body.title: Apply It: Calculate Your Safe Position Size
steps: Define your trading capital — the amount specifically allocated to futures trading
Apply the 1% risk rule: what is the maximum rupee amount you can lose on any single trade?
For a Nifty futures trade with a 100-point stop loss, how many lots does 1% risk allow?
For a Nifty futures trade with a 200-point stop loss, how many lots does 1% risk allow?
Calculate the total notional exposure for each scenario — compare to your capital
What leverage ratio results from proper position sizing vs the maximum leverage your broker allows?

lessons.title: F&O Taxation in India — What SEBI and the IT Department Require

children.text: F&O trading in India has specific tax treatment that most retail traders are unaware of until they receive a notice from the Income Tax department. The tax rules for F&O are entirely different from equity trading, and non-compliance — even innocent non-compliance — can lead to penalties, scrutiny, and tax demands. Understanding the rules before you start trading is not optional.
F&O Income Is Business Income

Unlike equity investing where gains are classified as capital gains, F&O profits and losses are treated as business income under the Income Tax Act. They are taxed at your applicable income tax slab rate. On the positive side, F&O losses can be set off against other business income, and losses can be carried forward for up to 8 years.

body.text: If your F&O turnover exceeds 1 crore rupees in a financial year, a tax audit by a chartered accountant is mandatory. F&O turnover is calculated not as your profit, but as the absolute sum of all your profits and losses on each trade. A trader who made 20 trades of 5,000 each in both directions has a turnover of 2 lakh even if net P&L is zero.

children.text: Advance Tax

If your total tax liability in a year exceeds 10,000 rupees, you must pay advance tax in quarterly instalments on June 15, September 15, December 15, and March 15. F&O traders who have profitable years must estimate their tax liability and pay advance tax, or face interest penalties on the shortfall under sections 234B and 234C of the Income Tax Act.

body.title: Apply It: Understand Your Tax Obligations
steps: Research: what is the current income tax slab applicable to your total annual income?
If you made 2 lakh rupees in F&O profits last year, calculate the tax payable at your slab rate
Research how F&O turnover is calculated — look up ICAI guidance or a reliable tax resource
Estimate: if you traded 100 lots of Nifty with an average gain or loss of 5,000 per trade, what would your turnover be?
Does that turnover trigger the audit requirement?
Consult a CA who specialises in F&O taxation before your first F&O trade

lessons.title: Famous Blowup: LTCM — When Genius Failed

children.text: In 1998, Long-Term Capital Management — a hedge fund run by two Nobel Prize-winning economists and a team of the most sophisticated financial minds on the planet — came within hours of collapsing the global financial system. They had built 1.25 trillion dollars in derivatives exposure on a capital base of 4 billion dollars. The leverage ratio was over 300 times. When their models failed, the US Federal Reserve had to organise a private sector bailout.
The Strategy That Seemed Infallible

LTCM's core strategy was convergence trading — identifying pairs of related assets where prices had diverged from historical relationships and betting they would converge back. For example, the yield spread between Italian government bonds and German government bonds had been historically stable. When it widened, LTCM bought Italian bonds and sold German bonds expecting the spread to narrow. The strategy had worked brilliantly for 4 years, generating 40 percent annual returns.

body.text: LTCM's fatal mistake was not the strategy — it was the leverage. Their risk models assumed markets were normally distributed and that past correlations would hold. When Russia defaulted in August 1998, global investors fled to safety simultaneously. All of LTCM's convergence positions moved against them at the same time. Their models had not accounted for the possibility that correlations between all asset classes could go to 1 in a crisis.

children.text: Lessons for Indian Futures Traders

Three lessons from LTCM apply directly to retail futures trading in India. First, past correlations and relationships can break down suddenly and without warning — never assume a pattern that has worked for years will continue. Second, leverage is the multiplier of both success and failure — the higher the leverage, the less room for error. Third, liquidity can disappear exactly when you need it most. The positions you think you can exit in a crisis may have no buyers at any reasonable price.

body.title: Apply It: Lessons from LTCM
steps: Research what happened to Nifty in March 2020 during the COVID crash — how many points did it fall in 3 weeks?
Calculate: if you had been long 5 lots of Nifty from 12000 to 7500, what would the loss have been?
Would that loss have wiped your trading capital?
Identify the specific risk management failures that led to LTCM's collapse
Apply each failure to your own trading: excessive leverage? Assuming relationships hold? Checking liquidity?
Write down how your current trading rules protect against each of these failures

lessons.title: Famous Blowup: Nick Leeson and the Fall of Barings Bank

children.text: In 1995, Nick Leeson — a 28-year-old derivatives trader at Barings Bank's Singapore office — single-handedly brought down Britain's oldest merchant bank, which had been operating since 1762. He did it by hiding massive losses in a secret account and doubling down on losing positions in Nikkei futures. The bank had 900 million pounds in capital. Leeson's losses exceeded 800 million pounds. Barings was sold to ING for 1 pound.
How It Started

Leeson's initial hiding of losses was small — a junior trader in his team had made a 20,000-pound error, and Leeson hid it in an account called 88888 to avoid embarrassment. This account became a repository for increasingly large losses as Leeson tried to trade his way out of the hole. The hole grew from 20,000 pounds to 800 million pounds over 2 years — all while Barings management believed Leeson was their star trader generating large profits.

body.text: The critical failure was risk management and oversight. Leeson controlled both the trading desk and the back office — he was marking his own positions and reporting his own P&L. No independent verification existed. A basic internal control principle — segregation of duties — was violated. The person trading must never be the same person reporting the results.

children.text: The Kobe Earthquake and the Final Doubling Down

By January 1995, Leeson was sitting on 200 million pounds of hidden losses. The Kobe earthquake struck Japan on January 17, sending Nikkei sharply lower. Instead of cutting losses, Leeson doubled down — buying massive quantities of Nikkei futures hoping for a recovery. The Nikkei continued falling. By February 1995, the losses were unrecoverable. The bank collapsed days later.

body.title: Apply It: Risk Control Lessons
steps: List the specific risk control failures that allowed Leeson's losses to compound for 2 years
For your own trading: does anyone else see your P&L independently of you reporting it?
Have you ever added to a losing position hoping for recovery? What happened?
Write down your personal rule for the maximum loss you will take on any single trade before closing it
Commit to a journal where you record every trade with entry, exit, and the honest reason for both decisions
Review your journal weekly — are you following your own rules consistently?

lessons.title: Your Futures Trading Rules — A Non-Negotiable Framework

children.text: After studying the mechanics of futures, the strategies, the pricing models, and the famous failures, it comes down to one thing: rules. Professional futures traders who survive and compound over years do so not because they are smarter than everyone else, but because they follow rules consistently. The rules are not complex. Applying them is the hard part — especially when your position is losing and every emotion is pushing you to break them.
The Non-Negotiable Rules

Rule 1: Never risk more than 1 to 2 percent of trading capital on a single trade. This ensures no single loss is catastrophic. Rule 2: Define stop loss before entry. Not after. Not when the trade moves against you. Before. And never widen a stop loss — only trail it toward entry as the trade works. Rule 3: Never average into a losing futures position. Exit, reassess, and re-enter if the setup is still valid.

Rule 4: Maintain a 30 percent buffer above minimum margin at all times. Never be in a position where a 1 percent adverse move triggers a margin call. Rule 5: After 3 consecutive losing trades, reduce position size by half until you return to breakeven. Losing streaks affect judgement — smaller size during streaks protects capital while you recover clarity.

body.text: The best futures traders are not those who are right most often — they are those who are right big and wrong small. A 40% win rate with average winner 3 times the average loser produces a positive expected value. Discipline in cutting losers and letting winners run is the actual edge, not market prediction ability.

children.text: Rollover Decisions

Roll a position forward only if the reason for the trade remains valid. If you are long Nifty futures because of a bullish technical setup and expiry arrives before the setup resolves, roll to next month only if the technical picture has not deteriorated. If the original reason is gone, exit at expiry and wait for the next setup. Do not roll simply because exiting feels like admitting a mistake.

body.title: Apply It: Write Your Trading Rules
steps: Write Rule 1: your maximum risk per trade as a specific rupee amount or percentage
Write Rule 2: your stop loss process — when do you define it and under what condition is it acceptable to exit before stop?
Write Rule 3: your averaging rule — will you ever add to a futures position? If yes, under what precise conditions?
Write Rule 4: your margin buffer rule — what is the minimum balance you will maintain above required margin?
Write Rule 5: your drawdown rule — at what point do you stop trading and review?
Print these rules and place them next to your trading terminal

lessons.title: Where to Go from Here — Connecting Futures to Options and Portfolio Hedging

children.text: You have now built a complete foundation in futures and derivatives. You understand what derivatives are, how futures are priced, how margin works, how strategies like directional trading and hedging are constructed, and what happens when risk management fails. The question now is: where does this knowledge take you next?
Futures and Options Together

Options and futures are not separate worlds — they are designed to be used together. A futures position can be protected with options: buy a put option to limit the downside of a long futures position, creating a synthetic call. Sell a call against a long futures position to generate income and reduce breakeven. Use options to structure positions with defined maximum loss that pure futures cannot offer.
Currency and Commodity Futures

The knowledge from equity futures transfers directly to currency futures on NSE — USD-INR, EUR-INR, GBP-INR. The mechanics are identical: lot size, margin, daily MTM, expiry, rollover. Currency futures allow you to hedge foreign currency exposure or express a view on the rupee's direction. Commodity futures on MCX — gold, silver, crude oil, copper — follow the same framework with different underlying assets.

body.text: The most powerful application of everything you have learned: portfolio-level risk management. Using Nifty futures to hedge equity exposure, options to create defined-risk positions, and currency futures to manage forex exposure — combining all three gives you institutional-grade risk management tools that most retail investors never access.

children.text: Your Learning Path Forward

The natural next step from this course is Options Trading from Zero — available in your course library. That course covers the complete options framework: Greeks, strategies, volatility, and multi-leg positions. Combined with what you have learned about futures, you will have a comprehensive derivatives education that most market participants — including many professionals — do not possess.

body.title: Apply It: Build Your Derivatives Learning Plan
steps: List all the concepts from this course that you feel confident about — rate yourself 1 to 5 on each major topic
List the concepts where you want more depth — margin mechanics, basis, hedging calculations
Set a specific goal: what do you want to be able to do with derivatives knowledge in 6 months?
Identify one real-world application: will you hedge your equity portfolio? Trade directionally? Learn options strategies?
Create a practice plan: paper trade futures for 30 days before risking real capital
After 30 days of paper trading, review your journal — what rules did you break and why?
